trick: Three commissions, three stages, three chairmen, and the dates run in order: Radhakrishnan 1948-49 for university education, Mudaliar 1952-53 for secondary, Kothari 1964-66 for the whole system. Kothari gave the 10+2+3 pattern and the phrase 'the destiny of India is now being shaped in her classrooms'.

chapter: National Policy on Education and the Three-Language Formula
trick: Two policies and one revision: NPE 1968 followed Kothari, NPE 1986 was revised in 1992, and NEP 2020 replaced them. The three-language formula means the regional language, Hindi and English — with the third language in Hindi-speaking states being a modern Indian language, usually from the south.

trick: One phrase each and they never blur. Tagore: freedom, nature and Santiniketan. Vivekananda: 'education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man', and man-making. Gandhi: Basic Education or Nai Talim, learning through a productive craft, in the mother tongue, self-supporting.

chapter: Western Educational Thinkers: Rousseau and Dewey
trick: Rousseau is the naturalist: Emile, follow nature, negative education, keep society away until the child is ready. Dewey is the pragmatist: education is life itself, not preparation for life, and the school is a miniature society where children learn by doing. Naturalism looks backward to nature, pragmatism forward to social use.

chapter: Delors Commission and the Four Pillars of Education
trick: Two dates, and questions confuse them: the Delors Commission was CONSTITUTED by UNESCO in 1993, and its report 'Learning: The Treasure Within' was PUBLISHED in 1996. The four pillars are learning to know, learning to do, learning to live together, and learning to be — the fourth is the one most often left out.

chapter: Right to Education Act and Constitutional Provisions
trick: Follow the sequence: Article 45 was a Directive Principle, the 86th Amendment of 2002 inserted Article 21A making education a fundamental right for ages 6 to 14, and the RTE Act 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010 to give it effect. A Directive Principle cannot be enforced in court; a fundamental right can — that is the whole significance of the change.

video.query: right to education act 2009 article 21A 86th amendment provisions class 12

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about the Right to Education.

items.statement: Article 21A makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14.
items.why: Inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002; below six, early childhood care remains a Directive Principle under Article 45.

items.statement: The RTE Act came into force on 1 April 2010.
items.why: Passed in 2009, it took effect the following financial year.

items.statement: The RTE Act requires private unaided schools to reserve 25% of Class I seats for disadvantaged children.
items.why: One of its most debated provisions, upheld by the Supreme Court.

items.statement: Before 2002, education was a fundamental right enforceable in court.
items.why: It was a Directive Principle under Article 45 — a moral direction to the state, not enforceable by a citizen.

items.statement: The RTE Act permits a school to detain a child before the end of the elementary stage.
items.why: The no-detention provision as originally enacted barred holding back or expelling a child up to Class VIII.

trick: Three words in ascending order of ambition: segregation puts children with disabilities in separate schools, integration places them in ordinary schools and expects them to cope, inclusion changes the school so that every child belongs. trick: Distance learning separates teacher and learner in space and time, and open learning removes the entry barriers — no age limit, no rigid qualification, learning at one's own pace. IGNOU (1985) is the national open university and NIOS the school-level board; questions usually want one of those two names.

video.query: open and distance learning IGNOU NIOS features class 12 education

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about open and distance learning.

items.statement: In distance education, teacher and learner are separated in space and often in time.
items.why: Printed material, broadcasts and online platforms carry the teaching instead of a classroom.

items.statement: 'Open' learning means the same thing as 'distance' learning.
items.why: Open refers to the removal of entry barriers — age, qualification, pace. A course can be open and face-to-face, or distance and highly restricted.

items.statement: IGNOU was established in 1985 and is a national open university.
items.why: It serves learners across the country and abroad through regional and study centres.

items.statement: NIOS provides open schooling up to the senior secondary stage.
items.why: It gives a second chance to those who could not complete school in the formal system.

items.statement: Distance education is unsuited to working adults.
items.why: It is designed for precisely them — flexible pace and no need to leave employment are among its chief advantages.

chapter: Educational Bodies: NCERT, NCTE and UNESCO
trick: Read the name and the work is inside it. NCERT researches and trains, so it writes the textbooks; NCTE regulates teacher education; UGC funds universities; UNESCO is the UN's education, science and culture body in Paris, founded 1946. None of them runs a school or awards a school certificate — that is the board's job.
